articles.title: The Memo: Tennessee debacle revives bitter debate over death penalty
articles.summary: The death penalty is back center stage in national politics in the most macabre of circumstances. Christa Pike, 50, who admits to the gruesome 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is in critical condition in the hospital after Tennessee’s attempt to execute her Wednesday evening failed. The attempted execution had only proceeded at the last…
articles.body:
The death penalty is back center stage in national politics in the most macabre of circumstances.

Christa Pike, 50, who admits to the gruesome 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is in critical condition in the hospital after Tennessee’s attempt to execute her Wednesday evening failed.

The attempted execution had only proceeded at the last minute when the Supreme Court cleared the way for it, overruling an earlier block from a federal appeals court.

Pike could be heard snoring even after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, the drug that was supposed to kill her, according to witnesses. She was taken by ambulance to the hospital where, as critics noted, the state that had just attempted to end her life then attempted to save it.

Pike’s attorneys said at a Thursday afternoon news conference that she was receiving “lifesaving medical care” but that they knew little about the specifics of her condition or her prognosis.

The political uproar was immediate after the distress and confusion of Wednesday’s events.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) said he was “highly disappointed” about what had taken place. He paused any further attempts to execute Pike for the moment and also announced that the one other execution scheduled in the state before the end of the year has been postponed. Lee has ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review” as to what exactly transpired.

Lee is about to be term-limited out of office, however. Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) is the GOP’s nominee to succeed him.

Blackburn wrote on social media that the situation with Pike was “tragic,” in part because she “should have been executed long ago.”

As for the failures of Wednesday evening, Blackburn had a suggested remedy: “The answer is simple: bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly. As your governor, I will do just that,” she wrote .

Blackburn’s Democratic opponent, Jerri Green, a member of the Memphis City Council, countered, “The fact of the matter is: the death penalty has always been inhumane, expensive, and biased.”

Green promised a moratorium on all future executions if elected governor and asserted , “If we say we are pro-life, that means we must be anti-death penalty.”

It would require a political earthquake for Green to get the chance to put her plans into practice, however. Most independent polls of the gubernatorial race put Blackburn up by more than 20 points in a state President Trump carried by 30 points in 2024.

Trump did not address the topic on social media and later said during a gaggle with reporters: “You’re going to have to speak to Tennessee about it.” The White House directed questions to the office of the Tennessee governor.

Such uncharacteristic reticence might, in part, be rooted in a disinclination to get involved in a disturbing controversy that has left all sides unhappy.

At Thursday’s news conference, one of Pike’s attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, alleged she had been “tortured in the execution chamber.” Calling for the commutation of her sentence, he added, “Tennessee should not be torturing its citizens in the name of justice.”

Another attorney for Pike, Randy Spivey, contended that the sequence of events Wednesday evening amounted to “cruel and unusual punishment.”

Campaigners against the death penalty believe the bleak sequence of events can cast new light on their cause.

“A death penalty process run by human beings has flaws at every stage, and what we have done is continuously ignore the flaws,” Laura Porter, the executive director of the U.S. Campaign to End the Death Penalty, told this column.

Porter acknowledged that polling indicates the American public supports the death penalty, albeit by a fairly small majority.

But, she contended, “when they see it up close, they come to the belief that it is not worth keeping. It is not an effective response to violence. This is a moment like that. This is an uncomfortable look at the realities of the death penalty.”

Amy Bergquist of the Advocates for Human Rights, which says it “implements international human rights standards to promote civil society and reinforce the rule of law,” made a similar point about specifics — including, in this case, the “protracted and horrific” abuse Pike herself had suffered in childhood. Pike’s defenders say this was overlooked at the time of her sentencing.

As for the difficulties with lethal injection, Bergquist added: “The whole purpose of what we call ‘lethal injection’ is really to help the public feel more at peace with a practice that is barbaric.”

Polling organization Gallup has the most reliable historical data on public attitudes to the death penalty — and it shows long-running shifts in trajectory.

After a brief moment in the mid-1960s when the death penalty lost majority support, backing for it grew to a peak in the mid-1990s, when crime rates were especially high. In 1994, 80 percent supported the death penalty and just 16 percent were opposed.

There has been a long erosion of support since then, however. Last year, 52 percent of Americans backed the death penalty and 44 percent were opposed.

As for executions themselves, they have been on the rise in the past few years after falling to a low of 11 nationwide in 2021, according to data from the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI). There were 47 executions last year, the highest figure since 2009.

Experts in the area note that one state — Florida — is responsible for much of the recent increase, however. The DPI data shows Florida executed 19 people last year , whereas no other state executed more than five people.

Those who want an end to the practice appear to be fighting an uphill battle, partly because of overall public opinion and partly because politicians have long feared being cast as “soft on crime.”

A generation ago, then-presidential candidate Bill Clinton was governor of Arkansas and returned home from the campaign trail for the execution of Ricky Ray Rector — a man whose mental impairment was severe enough that he said he would save the dessert from his last meal “for later.”

Still, efforts to abandon the practice continue.

In May, Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) reintroduced legislation to end the federal death penalty.

Reacting to the Pike case, Durbin wrote on social media Thursday:

“How many more failed executions must take place before this cruel practice is consigned to the dustbin of history? To paraphrase Supreme Court Justice Harry Blackmun: we must no longer tinker with the machinery of death.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.body:
Rep. Riley Moore (R-W.Va.) said Thursday that former President Nixon was “absolutely couped out of office” and added that he was “framed” during the infamous Watergate scandal .

“We now know more about the deep state and its power and ability to literally change things at the top,” the lawmaker said during his remarks at the Nixon Foundation’s annual Grand Strategy Summit in Washington.

“An interesting aspect of this as it relates to Richard Nixon — he knew all of this,” Moore continued. “He knew it, and he stayed quiet about it. Because he didn’t want to erode the confidence of the American people in our system of governance and our institutions.”

“The truth is now out there, so I think people feel a bit more liberated to talk about Richard Nixon and what an amazing president he was in this country,” he concluded.

The congressman’s remarks refer to a Wall Street Journal report that found the Department of Justice (DOJ) opened a review into whether the special prosecutor’s office committed misconduct while investigating the break-in at the Watergate Hotel, citing people familiar with the matter.

Former Nixon aide Geoff Shepard was also reportedly invited by a senior DOJ official to give a presentation at the department’s headquarters, per The Wall Street Journal. Shepard has repeatedly asserted since the 1972 scandal that Watergate was a plot to hide who Nixon’s Democratic donors were in his reelection campaign.

Moore compared President Trump to Nixon, who, he said, “faced this in his first term with the fake Russia collusion hoax and all that.”

The Senate Intelligence Committee released a report in 2020, finding significant contacts between the Trump campaign and Moscow during the 2016 election.

“Russia and other countries took advantage of the Transition Team’s inexperience, transparent opposition to Obama Administration policies, and Trump’s desire to deepen ties with Russia, to pursue unofficial channels through which Russia could conduct diplomacy,” the report reads, noting that this made the “transition open to influence and manipulation.”

The report followed a 22-month investigation by former special counsel Robert Mueller about possible collusion.

Trump bashed “ Radical Left Wing Media ” on social media in 2019 for “knowingly getting the Russia Collusion Delusion story so wrong” while Mueller was conducting his investigation.

articles.title: FBI arrests Energy Department employee accused of attempting to support Houthis
articles.summary: The FBI arrested a Department of Energy (DOE) employee Thursday at the Hanford, Wash., nuclear site under suspicion of trying to aid the Iranian-backed Houthi terrorist group in Yemen, according to the Justice Department. Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Wash., was charged with “attempting to provide material support or resources to the Houthis” after…
articles.body:
The FBI arrested a Department of Energy (DOE) employee Thursday at the Hanford, Wash., nuclear site under suspicion of trying to aid the Iranian-backed Houthi terrorist group in Yemen, according to the Justice Department.

Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Wash., was charged with “attempting to provide material support or resources to the Houthis” after he tried to help the group improve its communications capabilities, purchased materials for homemade explosives and drones and even traveled to Yemen, the department said .

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.

“Ellaboudy acquired materials for the construction of explosive material and drones capable of delivering these explosives,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said in a statement. “These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination.”

The FBI began to look into Ellaboudy after it received information that he had purchased precursor chemicals, components and other materials commonly used in the construction of homemade explosive devices. Their investigation also found he had purchased parts used to build drones and remotely operated aerial systems.

According to court documents, the FBI alleges that in December 2024 Ellaboudy took sick leave from his employment, “claiming that it was due to having been exposed to highly concentrated nitric acid, a common chemical used in the construction of explosive materials,” the Justice Department said.

Then in September 2025, Ellaboudy, using an official passport previously issued to him when employed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, traveled from Richland to Oman where he then crossed the border into Yemen. His alleged intent was to travel to Sanaa, the country’s capital, which is under the control of the Houthis.

Upon returning to the United States, Ellaboudy told U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers that he had traveled overseas on official government business, even though his DOE supervisor said he did not have any authorized official government travel to that region.

During the FBI’s investigation, Ellaboudy began communicating with a bureau source who claimed to be working for a Houthi “colonel” to acquire communications equipment that would be sent to Yemen for use in a mobile communications center.

“Ellaboudy provided expert advice and assistance, based upon his background in electrical engineering,” by helping the source test and modify solar power generators and communication equipment, the department said.

“Additionally, Ellaboudy provided guidance on how the power systems and communication system integrated, provided schematics and diagrams for the proper setup of the systems, and conducted research and provided guidance on other equipment that could be acquired to enhance the communications equipment of the Houthis,” according to the federal agency.

An Iranian proxy, the Houthis last month seized several towns and islands along Yemen’s western coast, which are crucial to controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

While the rebels have reportedly reassured the Trump administration that they won’t attack U.S. ships in the Red Sea, they have targeted Saudi Arabia with drones and ballistic missiles, prompting the kingdom to ask President Trump to launch strikes on the Houthis. Trump so far has rebuffed such pleas.

Hanford is the site of a costly and longstanding nuclear cleanup effort after it was originally established in the 1940s for the Manhattan Project. The complex now houses nearly 200 tanks containing 57 million gallons of high-level nuclear waste left over from weapons production.

The DOE stressed that Ellaboudy did not attempt to harm the Hanford site or its workforce and at no time was there a threat to the safety or security of the location.

articles.body:
This week, a set of bipartisan senators announced a major permitting reform bill aimed at speeding up the buildout of the nation’s infrastructure, especially energy projects, here’s what the bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), would actually do:

Limit environmental laws that hold back projects and restrict lawsuits:

A major component of the legislation is changes to the nation’s environmental laws that could make it easier to build projects and make it harder to block them, both with lawsuits and other legal mechanisms.

One of the biggest changes are limits that restrict lawsuits against projects, mandating that they be filed within 150 days of a project’s approval. It also limits lawsuits to only those who weighed in publicly if the project has a public comment period and those who may be directly harmed by a project.

The changes are contentious, with supporters saying the change will cut down on lawsuits that can interrupt a project years after it is approved while opponents say the short window could prevent legitimate complaints.

The bill also has provisions that are expected to make it easier to build and approve power lines in particular, which is key to getting more power onto the grid. Democrats have pushed for such reforms, saying they believe they will particularly bolster renewable energy.

“The bill overall has a particularly strong impact on getting transmission built and otherwise expanding transmission capacity with new technologies,” said Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies LLC.

articles.title: Few Americans associate their elected leaders with the term ‘courage’: Gallup
articles.summary: When asked to select which category of people they most associated with courage, 4 percent of Americans selected elected officials — tying with social media influencers, according to newly-published Gallup survey results. In the new poll, released Wednesday, respondents were given a list of 16 different groups of people — such as first responders, scientists,…
articles.body:
When asked to select which category of people they most associated with courage, 4 percent of Americans selected elected officials — tying with social media influencers, according to newly-published Gallup survey results.

In the new poll, released Wednesday, respondents were given a list of 16 different groups of people — such as first responders, scientists, teachers and the average American. Gallup then asked them to pick three they saw as most linked to courage, which it defined as “deciding to do what’s right in the face of personal cost,” and three they associated with the word the least.

Four percent of respondents selected “elected leaders in the U.S. government” as a group they saw as most linked to courage, tying with influencers and passing up both business leaders and athletes — which 2 percent of those polled associated with the trait. The top responses included first responders at 60 percent, military personnel at 41 and nurses at 27.

Fifty-four percent of respondents elected officials as the category they saw as least tied to courage — the most common response to the question.

Gallup’s fresh poll also comes as Americans express a lack of faith in their country’s leadership, with President Trump’s approval rating sitting at 37.5 percent as of Thursday evening. This figure hit a career low for Trump last week, dipping to 32 percent.

Americans also appear frustrated with Republican’s Congressional leadership in Washington, with some Democratic candidates taking unexpected leads on the generic ballot, as well as in races in traditionally red or purple states, ahead of November’s midterms.

The Gallup poll took place from May 12 to 22, featuring 3,199 respondents and a margin of error of 2.1 percentage points.

articles.body:
Medicare de-fangs new drug pricing model

The Trump administration rolled out the final version of a new Medicare payment model aimed at lowering the prices of drugs administered in doctors’ offices to match those paid in countries overseas.

President Trump has made lower drug prices a signature part of his administration’s affordability agenda. The Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing (GLOBE) model requires drug companies to offer a rebate if a price exceeds rates in certain countries.

But the final version is significantly scaled back from when it was first proposed.

It’s now estimated that the GLOBE model will save $440 million over seven years — a 96 percent reduction from the proposed version, which estimated nearly $12 billion in savings over the same period.

The payment model is mandatory, but there is a myriad of exemptions , most notably if a company entered a separate deal with the White House for “most-favored-nation” pricing in Medicaid.

In the end, only three companies are covered by the final model, a decrease from about 40 firms estimated in the proposed rule.

“The government has crafted it in such a way that it will touch almost no drugs and deliver almost no savings,” drug industry consultant Brian Reid wrote Wednesday.

To qualify for GLOBE, a drug must account for more than $100 million in traditional Medicare Part B spending per year.

The final version of the model only covers a handful of drugs ; Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) now estimates that less than 1 percent of eligible Part B drug spending is initially targeted by GLOBE.

“At CMS, we’re focused on more than promises to make healthcare more affordable — we’re taking action to pilot a new approach to lower costs and strengthen the quality of care while preserving medical innovation,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said in a statement.
